title: Generative AI in K-12 Education: The CyberScholar Initiative
extended_summary:
This paper examines whether CyberScholar, a generative AI writing assistant, can support K-12 students’ writing through formative feedback aligned to teachers’ rubrics, instructional materials, and classroom expectations. The central research question is: to what extent does CyberScholar have the potential to support students’ writing across subject areas? The study is positioned as a response to concerns about declining writing performance and the limited evidence on how generative AI feedback functions in secondary school settings.

The intervention was a pilot implementation of CyberScholar, a GenAI-based tool that used retrieval-augmented generation and prompt engineering to incorporate teachers’ rubrics, prompts, and classroom materials into the feedback process. Students submitted drafts, received AI-generated formative feedback, and in some cases asked follow-up questions and resubmitted revised work. The paper emphasizes the tool’s design as pedagogically guided rather than generic AI use, with feedback intended to mirror teacher expectations and support iterative revision.

The study was conducted in four U.S. public schools: three high schools and one middle school, across the Midwest and Northwest. Participants included 121 students and 4 teachers in grades 7, 8, 10, and 11, across English Language Arts, Social Studies, and Modern World History classes. Data collection included observations, surveys, and interviews, with thematic analysis of qualitative data. Although all 121 students participated in implementation, only 54 students and 3 teachers completed the post-survey, and 8 students plus 1 teacher participated in interviews.

The main conclusions are that students and teachers perceived CyberScholar as a useful support for writing, especially because it provided detailed and specific feedback, interactive clarification, rubric-linked ratings, and guidance for revision. Students reported perceived improvements in areas such as grammar, transitions, conclusions, sentence clarity, and argument presentation. However, the study did not include a control group or objective comparative outcome measures, and some students reported inconsistent ratings from the tool. The authors conclude that CyberScholar shows promise as a complement to, not a replacement for, teacher feedback, but broader and more rigorous research is needed.
quality_tier_rationale: This is an exploratory qualitative multiple-case pilot with convenience sampling, low post-survey response rates, and no control/comparison condition or validated pre-post outcome analysis. It provides useful implementation evidence but only one of the key credibility criteria for stronger causal inference.
impact_tier_rationale: Findings suggest promising but unclear impact: students reported perceived improvements in writing and engagement, but no standardized outcome effects or causal estimates were provided. For the target question on comparative effectiveness of ChatGPT-style feedback versus teacher/peer/other feedback, the evidence is adjacent and insufficient to estimate magnitude.

interventions.use_case: CyberScholar provides rubric-aligned formative feedback on student writing drafts across grades 7, 8, 10, and 11 in ELA, social studies, and history, including ratings tied to teacher rubrics and suggestions for revision.
CyberScholar includes an interactive dialogue feature allowing students to ask follow-up questions about feedback and receive elaborated explanations during revision.
The tool functions as a generative AI writing assistant that suggests improvements to grammar, sentence structure, transitions, argument clarity, and professional tone in student essays.

finding.finding_summary: In this exploratory qualitative pilot, students generally perceived CyberScholar as helpful for improving writing quality, especially through detailed feedback on grammar, transitions, conclusions, sentence clarity, and argument presentation. Evidence is based on self-reports and illustrative rubric-score improvements for individual cases rather than controlled comparisons; among 54 post-survey respondents, 23 explicitly said the tool helped them improve their writing, and 36 said they would use it again.
finding.measure: Student post-survey comments, interviews, classroom observations, and anecdotal rubric-linked revision improvements on writing assignments
finding.study_size: n=121 participants overall; n=54 student/teacher post-survey respondents; 8 students interviewed

finding.finding_summary: Qualitative findings suggest the tool may support metacognition and self-regulated revision by making rubric criteria visible, enabling iterative resubmission, and allowing students to ask clarifying follow-up questions. Students described using the feedback to identify where to focus revisions and to track improvement across drafts, but no validated metacognition or self-regulation measures were reported.
finding.measure: Qualitative reports of self-directed learning, iterative revision behavior, rubric-focused reflection, and interactive questioning
finding.study_size: n=121 participants overall; n=54 post-survey respondents; 8 students interviewed

finding.finding_summary: Students showed generally positive engagement with the tool, with 36 post-survey respondents saying they would like to use CyberScholar again, and some reporting that rubric-linked star ratings motivated further revision. However, 11 students were hesitant to use the tool again, and some expressed frustration over inconsistent ratings for unchanged submissions, indicating uneven effects on confidence and trust.
finding.measure: Post-survey willingness to reuse the tool, motivational reactions to ratings, and qualitative interview/survey comments about satisfaction and frustration

finding.finding_summary: The study reports perceived efficiency benefits from rapid, detailed feedback that students could access independently during revision, and the discussion frames the tool as potentially supporting teacher workload by providing timely rubric-aligned comments. These findings are perception-based only; no direct time-on-task, turnaround-time, or workload metrics were collected.
finding.measure: Qualitative perceptions of speed, convenience, and usefulness relative to peer/self-review and teacher feedback processes
finding.study_size: n=121 participants overall; qualitative subset not fully disaggregated

finding.finding_summary: Teachers and authors describe the tool as potentially shifting teacher roles from sole evaluators to facilitators of AI-supported feedback loops and as a possible mechanism for improving access to formative feedback across differently resourced schools. However, these are interpretive implementation observations rather than measured institutional outcomes.
finding.measure: Teacher interviews, implementation observations, and author thematic analysis of role shifts and equity/access implications
finding.study_size: n=4 teachers overall; 3 teacher post-survey respondents; 1 teacher interviewed
